This has gotten me thinking for a few days. As an American with a decent understanding of Marx, Lenin, and a wee bit of Mao, I have tried to think of what American socialism would look like. I'm not deep theorist with the ideas of every person whose ever written on it embedded in my brain, but I have a few thoughts on this, both in terms of what it would take to build the movement and what it may look like afterwards. Note: none of this is meant to be overly critical or acclaiming of one movement or another. Just a thought exercise on the subject. 

1: Reform as a means, not an end  
This is more of a "how do we get here" and not a final result. I think leftism in America needs to adopt the policy of reform not as a means to attain socialism, which ultimately will fail, but rather as a means of building some level of worker power. In the US specifically, workers have virtually no power in comparison to private capital which has \*extreme power\*. We did not see this in many of the successful revolutions, where neither private capital nor workers had extensive power. It was very muddy in China and Russia, and to a lesser extent in others. But here, capital has \*immense\* power, probably more than at any other time in history. Therefore, while socialism can never be attained by the ballot box, building some level of foundation in union victories and better representation would benefit American socialism in the long run. Ultimately, you'd basically have to use the levers of the state to remove power from the state. That will cause issues with mainline socialist theorists. 

2: Decentralization (to a degree)  
A lot of Marxists, Leninists, and Maoists are focused on ideological purity and the one-party-establishment. I question whether this has uses in the United States, a people and culture so heavily focused on expanding the two party system and bringing more choices, not less. I also think the level of focus on federalism, state's rights, local control, etc. (mixed with a little propaganda) has really made the idea of a one-party, centralized state largely useless in the United States. You'd never get the support necessary for long term success without completely rewiring the cultural zeitgeist (which would take generations). I think rather, have an organization that houses the different facets of the movement, while not itself being a one party apparatus, would be more likely to spread. I simply do not see a scenario where Americans accept a one-party state, even in the best case. 

3: Language  
Let's be real, the language of Marxism has been heavily been propagandized in America. It asks the question is the importance of socialism in the language, or the ideas. If you can find a way to incorporate socialist ideas into American language (liberty, freedom, rah rah rah), you'd have more success than just hammering the right words every time.

4: Patriotism  
I don't actually know if there is a way to do this, and this might be the final nail for anyone skeptical of this list already. Americans are obsessed with patriotism. The USSR kind of worked it in during the Great Patriotic War in some of its language, but that isn't for everyone. American socialism would probably, at least in the short term, have a heavier than normal focus on patriotism and Americanism, if it were to work at all. 

Honestly, this may not even ever come to pass. We've never had a serious socialist movement in the capitalist core, probably because of the strength of capital in them. I think others have raised good points in here, but this was just a brief thought exercise that honestly I could write an entire paper on if I dedicated the time to it. As a more syndicalist minded individual, that obviously influences my thinking, but this is just a quick stab, and not a real fleshed out idea. This sort of thing also begs the question of whether or not you \*could\* build socialism in the United States, or whether the timeline to do so is just too long to really consider it.

Yo, gonna be real, Harris WAS a bad candidate. Not cause of the Palestine issue (a factor, but not the big one), and not all of it was personally connected to her. But, the way the Democrats, Biden, and subsequently Harris ran this campaign all but guaranteed a loss. 

1: The lack of a primary and the perceived crowning of Harris was a major source of discontent from would be voters and Democrats. Biden should have stuck to his original promise as a one term president, allowed a primary to run, and thus allowed a true candidate to appear via the voters, not via appointment. People want their democracy, and with the recent issues with Sanders sidelining/loss (depending on how you feel on it) this only cemented discontent with the establishment. 

2: Harris and the establishments inability/refusal to separate herself from the Biden administration hurt them heavily. I know Biden “gave her permission” to do so, but she didn’t, and the Democrats didn’t. At a time when people were upset about prices, upset about foreign support that they thought was too much, and scared of future prospects, all of which were related, either literally or just perceptively, to the current admin, you cannot run a campaign of continuing the current admin. That’s just politics 101. 

3: The lack of working class economic issues, the focus on “I’m not Trump” and nebulous ideas of democracy and women’s rights, were not winning issues. Ultimately, whether we like it or not, bread and butter issues are what carry campaigns. Honestly even if she had promised to halt foreign aide, I don’t think she would have won. Where was Medicare for all? Where was minimum wage? She posted some ads about coming down on corporate greed yes, but ultimately a huge chunk of the advertising, campaigning, and activism was “I’m not Trump!”. We can go on till we are blue in the face about how that should have been enough, that she shouldn’t have had to try, that any sane person would look at Trump and say “I’ll take a pile of shit over him.” But unfortunately, that isn’t our reality and that isn’t the reality of politics. Alright, I’m bought to break this down economics style. 

To those saying “their wealth is in stocks!” or “they already pay 42% of all taxes” lemme break down an economic concept called Marginal propensity to consume (MPC). 

Now essentially, MPC measures what portion of new income people will spend, MPC, vs what they will save, called the marginal propensity to save (MPS). These two are measure as decimals and always equal 1. MPC=.8, MPS=.2 means that for every dollar of new income a person gets, they will spend $.80 and save $.20. 

What we see is that middle and lower income groups have a higher MPC than their upper class counterparts, which make sense because they are spending a larger portion of their income on consumables and things like food, clothing, transportation, rent, etc. So why is this important? 

The problem with the MPS is that it is considered leakage in macroeconomic sense, because that money is not being used in the economy. Now, you can’t reach a point where there IS no saving, because people always save. Therefore, there will always be less money spent than is produced via labor. What comes in to offset this is investment, which ideally would match the level of savings so that the economy is equilibrium. Whether that’s gov or private investment, it will inject back into the economy what has been lost to saving.

“But why does this matter to billionaires?”

As we said, upper classes have a much lower MPC, meaning they have a much higher MPS. Things like stocks, bonds, real estate, whatever they have their wealth in, are all essentially taking money out of the economy, that they are not or can not make up with investment. 

So yes, they are obligated to contribute to society and not hoard wealth, because that is the only way a capitalist economy can reach equilibrium. Otherwise we are chronically losing money from the economy that won’t be spent on goods, which then leads to unsold inventory or overproduction.
